lessons.title: KMP String Matching Algorithm
lessons.objective: Implement KMP string matching in O(n+m) by building a failure function that encodes how far to backtrack without losing valid progress after a mismatch.
concepts: Naive string matching: O(n*m) due to redundant comparisons after mismatch
KMP insight: after a mismatch, use already-matched characters to avoid re-comparison
Failure function (lps array): lps[i] = length of longest proper prefix of pattern[0..i] that is also a suffix
lps[0] = 0 (single character has no proper prefix/suffix)
Build lps in O(m): two-pointer approach tracking matched prefix length
Matching: on mismatch, jump pattern pointer using lps, not text pointer
O(n+m) total: text pointer never moves backward
Application: Find All Occurrences of Pattern in Text
lessons.explanation: KMP (Knuth-Morris-Pratt) achieves O(n+m) string matching by precomputing a failure function (also called lps = longest proper prefix which is also suffix). The lps array for the pattern encodes: after matching lps[i] characters of the pattern starting from position 0, if a mismatch occurs at pattern position i+1, we already know the longest valid prefix of the pattern that we have matched (lps[i] characters), so we jump the pattern pointer back to lps[i] instead of position 0. Building lps: use two pointers l (current matching length) and r (scanning position). If pattern[l] == pattern[r], lps[r] = l+1, advance both. If mismatch and l > 0, jump l back to lps[l-1] (reuse previously computed values). Matching: maintain a pattern pointer j. For each text character: if match, advance both. On mismatch, jump j to lps[j-1]. Never move the text pointer backward, giving O(n) text scans. Total O(n+m).
lessons.analogy: KMP is like reading a book where if you lose your place, instead of going back to page 1, you know the furthest back you could have drifted. The lps array is your 'minimum restart page' for each position in the chapter you have memorised (the pattern). A mismatch does not mean starting over from scratch — it means jumping back to the furthest position where the memorised text could still match.

code_example.explanation: The lps array construction reuses the same two-pointer logic as the matching phase. When pattern[l] != pattern[r] and l > 0, we do NOT reset l to 0. Instead we jump l = lps[l-1]. This reuses previously computed overlap information and ensures the O(m) build time.

common_mistakes: Resetting l to 0 on mismatch instead of l = lps[l-1] — this makes lps construction O(m²); the jump to lps[l-1] is what gives O(m) build time by reusing previously computed prefix-suffix overlaps
Moving the text pointer backward on pattern mismatch — in the matching phase, the text pointer i should NEVER move backward; only the pattern pointer j is reset using lps[j-1]
Using lps[j] instead of lps[j-1] on mismatch — after a mismatch at position j, the valid prefix we have matched is of length j (not j+1); lps[j-1] gives the length of the next longest valid prefix
lessons.interview_relevance: KMP appears directly in Shortest Palindrome (#214, NeetCode 150): the shortest palindrome is formed by finding the longest palindromic prefix of s, which reduces to KMP on the string s + '#' + reverse(s). Repeated String Match (#686) and Index of First Occurrence (#28) are direct KMP applications. KMP is expected at companies with heavy string processing (search engines, bioinformatics).

flashcards.front: KMP: what problem does it solve and at what complexity?
flashcards.back: Pattern matching: find ALL occurrences of pattern P (length m) in text T (length n) in O(n+m). Naive: O(n×m). KMP avoids re-scanning text characters by using precomputed failure function to skip redundant comparisons.

flashcards.front: KMP failure function lps[i]: what does it represent?
flashcards.back: lps[i] = length of the longest PROPER prefix of P[0..i] that is also a suffix of P[0..i]. 'Proper' means not the full string itself. Example: P='AABAAB', lps=[0,1,0,1,2,3]. lps[5]=3 because 'AAB' (length 3) is both a prefix and suffix of 'AABAAB'.

flashcards.front: KMP failure function: how is it computed?
flashcards.back: lps[0]=0 (base). Use two pointers len=0, i=1. While i<m: if P[i]==P[len]: lps[i]=len+1, len++, i++. Else if len>0: len=lps[len-1] (fallback, don't increment i). Else: lps[i]=0, i++. O(m) total.

flashcards.front: KMP search: what happens on a mismatch at pattern position j>0?
flashcards.back: Don't reset j to 0 (that wastes work). Instead: j = lps[j-1] (jump back using the failure function). This skips the redundant prefix-check because we KNOW the last lps[j-1] characters of the text already matched the pattern prefix of that length.

flashcards.front: KMP: when is a match found?
flashcards.back: When j (pattern index) reaches m: a complete match ending at text position i-1. Add i-m to results. Then: j = lps[m-1] to continue searching (don't reset to 0 — there may be overlapping matches).

flashcards.front: lps array for P='ABABCAB': what is lps[4]?
flashcards.back: P[0..4]='ABABC'. Proper prefixes: '', 'A', 'AB', 'ABA', 'ABAB'. Proper suffixes: 'ABABC', 'BABC', 'ABC', 'BC', 'C'. Longest proper prefix that's also a suffix: '' (length 0). lps[4]=0. (C doesn't match A, and no shorter prefix matches a suffix.)

quiz.question: KMP lps for P='AABAAAB': lps[5]=? P[0..5]='AABAAA'
quiz.explanation: P[0..5]='AABAAA'. Proper prefixes that are also suffixes: 'AA' (length 2) — 'AA' is the first two chars and also the last two chars of 'AABAAA'. Does 'AAB' work? 'AAB' vs 'AAA': no. 'AA' works. lps[5]=2.

quiz.question: KMP mismatch at j=4, lps=[0,0,1,2,3]. Next j?
quiz.explanation: j=4 mismatch: j = lps[j-1] = lps[3] = 2. Wait: lps[3]=2. So j becomes lps[4-1]=lps[3]=2. Answer: j=2. The failure function lookup is lps[j-1] = lps[3] = 2.

quiz.question: KMP search for P='ABA' in T='ABABABA': how many matches?
quiz.explanation: Matches starting at indices 0, 2, 4. After finding match at 0 (j reaches 3=m): j=lps[2]=1 (not 0, enabling overlap). Continue: j=1 at text[3]='B', match → j=2 at text[4]='A', match → j=3, record match at 4-3=2... Actually: T='ABABABA' (7 chars), P='ABA' (3 chars). Matches at indices 0, 2, 4. Count=3.

quiz.question: Why does KMP achieve O(n+m) while naive is O(nm)?
options: KMP uses hashing
KMP never backtracks the text pointer — each text character is processed at most once; the pattern pointer uses lps to skip redundant comparisons
KMP uses binary search on the text
KMP only works on sorted text
quiz.explanation: KMP's key invariant: the text pointer i only moves FORWARD. When a mismatch occurs, only the pattern pointer j jumps back (via lps). Since i never decreases: total text-character comparisons ≤ n. lps computation: O(m). Total: O(n+m).

theory_mcq.question: The LPS (failure function) array encodes 'longest proper prefix of pattern[0..i] that is also a suffix'. Why does this property enable O(n+m) matching by PREVENTING text pointer backtracking?
options: LPS prevents backtracking by caching previously computed match results

After a MISMATCH at position j in the pattern (text[i] ≠ pattern[j]): instead of moving text pointer back and restarting, we jump the PATTERN pointer to lps[j-1]; this works because lps[j-1] characters at the start of the pattern ALREADY MATCH the same number of characters ending at text[i-1] (by definition of lps); we skip re-matching those characters; the text pointer never decrements; each text character is processed at most twice (once when matching, once when advancing past a mismatch) = O(n) text processing; O(m) for building lps = O(n+m) total
LPS allows skipping text characters that cannot possibly match the pattern
LPS works by hashing previously seen substrings to avoid recomputation
theory_mcq.explanation: Matching the lesson's concept: 'KMP insight: after a mismatch, use already-matched characters to avoid re-comparison' and 'O(n+m) total: text pointer never moves backward' — the lps value tells us: 'you've already verified these first lps[j-1] characters of the pattern match what just came before in the text'; jumping to lps[j-1] reuses this verified information without re-scanning the text.

theory_mcq.question: For pattern 'aabaab', the LPS array is [0,1,0,1,2,3]. What does lps[5]=3 mean?
options: lps[5]=3 means the pattern has 3 characters total

lps[5]=3 means: the LONGEST PROPER PREFIX of 'aabaab' (the full pattern, length 6) that is also a SUFFIX has length 3; that prefix/suffix is 'aab' (pattern[0..2]='aab' = pattern[3..5]='aab'); 'proper' means strictly shorter than the full string (lengths 1..5 considered); this tells the matching algorithm: after matching all 6 characters and then finding another mismatch at the next position, we already know 3 characters of the pattern match — start from position 3
lps[5]=3 means position 3 is the next position to check
lps[5]=3 means the pattern has 3 unique characters
theory_mcq.explanation: Confirmed by direct execution: lps for 'aabaab' = [0,1,0,1,2,3]; lps[5]=3 means 'aabaab'[0..2]='aab' matches 'aabaab'[3..5]='aab' — 'aab' is both a prefix and suffix of length 3; when a match of the full pattern is found and we look for the next match, we jump the pattern pointer to 3 (lps[5]=3), preserving the already-matched 'aab' prefix.

logic_mcq.question: For `kmpSearch('aabxaabaab', 'aab')`, the correct result is [0,4,7]. Verify that 'aab' appears at index 4.
options: text='aabxaabaab'; text[4..6]='aab' ✓ (text[4]='a', text[5]='a', text[6]='b'); also text[0..2]='aab' and text[7..9]='aab' — three occurrences at [0,4,7]
text[5..7]='aba' — the pattern starts at index 5, not 4
The pattern appears at indices [0,5,7] — the lesson's claimed output
There are only two occurrences at [0,7]
logic_mcq.explanation: Confirmed by both direct execution ([0,4,7]) and manual verification: text='aabxaabaab' (0-indexed); text[0..2]='aab'✓, text[4..6]='aab'✓ (text[4]='a',text[5]='a',text[6]='b'), text[7..9]='aab'✓; text[5..7]='aba'✗ (NOT 'aab'); the lesson's console comment claiming [0,5,7] is incorrect — the verified answer is [0,4,7].

logic_mcq.question: In the lps BUILD algorithm, when `pattern[r] !== pattern[l]` and `l > 0`, we set `l = lps[l-1]` (not `l = 0`). Why backtrack l using lps rather than resetting to 0?
options: Resetting l=0 also works; using lps is only an optimisation

AVOIDS O(m²) BUILD: resetting l=0 is naive and would require rechecking all previous characters; the insight: if pattern[0..l-1] was a proper prefix/suffix match and pattern[l]≠pattern[r], we can try matching a SHORTER prefix; the longest prefix that could still match (ending at l-1) is given by lps[l-1]; this avoids re-comparing characters we've already seen; this is exactly the same insight as KMP matching applied to the LPS BUILD itself — building lps is essentially running KMP on the pattern against itself
lps[l-1] gives the next character to compare, not a backtrack position
Backtracking with lps only works when the pattern has repeated characters
logic_mcq.explanation: Matching the lesson's code: `else if(l>0) l=lps[l-1]` — the lps BUILD is O(m) for the same reason KMP matching is O(n): l never increases faster than r and can only backtrack through lps values, giving amortised O(1) per step; resetting l=0 would be O(m²) in the worst case (consider pattern 'aaaab').

syntax_mcq.question: In KMP matching, after a full pattern match (`j === m`), the next pattern position is `j = lps[j-1]`. What enables OVERLAPPING MATCHES this way?
options: After a match, j is always reset to 0 regardless of lps

lps[j-1] gives the LENGTH OF THE LONGEST PROPER PREFIX of the full pattern that is also a suffix; after finding a match ending at text[i-1], the suffix of the matched text positions that equals the pattern's lps[m-1]-length prefix can SERVE AS THE START of the next potential match; jumping to lps[m-1] instead of 0 allows the algorithm to find overlapping matches (e.g., 'aa' in 'aaaa': after matching 'aa' at position 0, lps[1]=1, so j=1 enables matching 'aa' again starting at position 1)
Overlapping matches require special-casing; KMP cannot find them by default
j=lps[j-1] only matters for patterns with repeated characters
syntax_mcq.explanation: Matching the lesson's code: `j = lps[j-1]` after a match — for 'aa' in 'aaaa': lps=['0','1']; after first match at i=2, j=2, j=lps[1]=1; now j=1 means we've already matched 1 character of the next potential match; this finds the overlapping match at position 1; kmpSearch('aaaa','aa')=[0,1,2] confirmed by direct execution.

lessons.title: Rabin-Karp Rolling Hash
lessons.objective: Implement Rabin-Karp rolling hash in O(n+m) average for single-pattern matching and O(n + Σm_i) for multiple-pattern matching, and handle hash collisions correctly.
concepts: Rolling hash: hash of window slides in O(1) by removing oldest character and adding newest
Polynomial hash: hash = sum(c_i * base^i) mod prime
Rolling: remove leftmost char, add rightmost char in O(1)
Hash collision: two different strings with the same hash (false positive)
Verify on hash match: O(m) character comparison to confirm true match
O(n+m) average: O(m) hash match verification is rare for good hash functions
Multiple patterns: store pattern hashes in a Set; O(n) scan with O(1) Set lookup
Double hashing: use two different primes to reduce collision probability
lessons.explanation: Rabin-Karp uses a rolling hash for O(n) sliding window matching after O(m) preprocessing. The polynomial hash of a string s[0..m-1]: H = (s[0]*b^(m-1) + s[1]*b^(m-2) + ... + s[m-1]*b^0) mod p, where b is a base (e.g., 31 for lowercase letters) and p is a large prime. Rolling: to slide from window [i, i+m-1] to [i+1, i+m]: remove s[i]*b^(m-1), multiply remaining by b, add s[i+m]. This is O(1) per slide. When the window hash matches the pattern hash, verify with O(m) character comparison (to avoid false positives from hash collisions). For good hash functions, collisions are rare, giving O(n+m) average time. Rabin-Karp excels at multiple-pattern matching: compute hashes of all patterns and store in a Set. For each text window, compute the hash in O(1) and check the Set in O(1). This gives O(n + Σm_i) total where Σm_i is the total length of all patterns.
lessons.analogy: Rabin-Karp rolling hash is like a rolling fingerprint detector in a security system. Instead of comparing the entire suspect profile (string comparison), you compare a compressed fingerprint (hash). If fingerprints match, you then compare the full profile to confirm (collision check). The fingerprint slides across the input — as one person leaves the frame, another enters, and the fingerprint updates instantly.

code_example.explanation: The +MOD in the rolling hash formula (winHash - ... + MOD) % MOD prevents negative values in JavaScript, since JavaScript's % operator can return negative values for negative operands. Adding MOD before taking the final modulus ensures the hash stays in [0, MOD-1].

common_mistakes: Not verifying on hash match (accepting hash equality as a true match) — hash collisions are rare but real; always verify with O(m) character comparison on hash match; omitting verification produces wrong answers
Not adding MOD when computing the rolling subtraction — the subtraction (winHash - text[i]*highPow) can be negative; always add MOD before taking modulus: (winHash - x + MOD) % MOD
Using a weak hash base (e.g., base=1) or a small prime — this dramatically increases collision probability; use base=31 for lowercase letters and a large prime like 10^9+7
lessons.interview_relevance: Rabin-Karp appears in Longest Duplicate Substring (#1044, NeetCode 150), where binary search on the substring length combined with rolling hash gives O(n log n) total. It is also the natural choice for 'find all occurrences of multiple patterns' problems. The rolling hash technique is a fundamental tool that appears in many advanced string problems.

flashcards.front: Rabin-Karp: core idea?
flashcards.back: Compute a ROLLING HASH of the current text window of length m. Compare hash to pattern hash. If equal, verify with string comparison. Slide the window: remove leftmost char, add rightmost char in O(1). Expected O(n+m); worst case O(nm) if many hash collisions.

flashcards.front: Rabin-Karp rolling hash formula: removing leftmost, adding rightmost?
flashcards.back: hash = (hash - arr[i] × base^(m-1)) × base + arr[i+m]. All mod a large prime. Multiply by base (shifts digits left), subtract leftmost contribution, add new rightmost character. The precomputed power base^(m-1) enables O(1) slide.

flashcards.front: Rabin-Karp: why use modular arithmetic?
flashcards.back: Polynomial hash values can exceed 64-bit integers for large strings. Modular arithmetic keeps values bounded. Tradeoff: introduces hash collisions (different strings with same hash mod p). Using two independent hash functions (double hashing) reduces collision probability to ~1/p².

flashcards.front: Rabin-Karp: Longest Duplicate Substring (#1044) approach?
flashcards.back: Binary search on length L. For each L: compute rolling hashes of all substrings of length L, store in a set. If any hash appears twice: potential duplicate (verify to handle collisions). Binary search over L: O(n log n) total.

flashcards.front: Rabin-Karp vs KMP: when to prefer each?
flashcards.back: KMP: single pattern search, guaranteed O(n+m), no collisions. Rabin-Karp: multiple pattern search (add all pattern hashes to a set, check each window once) in O(n+m total), or binary search on length like #1044. For single pattern: KMP is more reliable (no collision risk).

flashcards.front: Rabin-Karp: how to handle the modular inverse when subtracting?
flashcards.back: hash - arr[i] × base^(m-1) can be negative mod p. Fix: add p before taking mod: (hash - arr[i] × pow_val % p + p) % p. The +p ensures the result is non-negative before the final mod.

quiz.question: Rolling hash: window 'ABC' → 'BCD' (slide right). If hash('ABC')=42, base=31, p=101, value of 'D'=4, value of 'A'=1, base^2=961 mod 101 = 658? Too complex. Simpler: which step is NOT part of sliding the window?
options: Subtract contribution of leftmost character
Multiply remaining hash by base
Add contribution of new rightmost character
Sort the characters in the window
quiz.explanation: The three steps of rolling hash: (1) remove leftmost char contribution, (2) multiply by base (shift), (3) add new rightmost char. Sorting is never part of rolling hash — it would destroy position information.

quiz.question: Rabin-Karp finds a hash match but the strings don't match. This is called?
options: A true positive
A false positive (hash collision)
A false negative
An overflow error
quiz.explanation: Hash collision: two different strings have the same hash value. Rabin-Karp always verifies with direct string comparison after a hash match to handle false positives. A missed true match (false negative) cannot occur with a correct hash implementation.

quiz.question: Rabin-Karp multiple pattern search with k patterns: total time?
options: O(n×k×m) — check each pattern at each position
O(n×m + k×m) — O(nm) rolling hash + k pattern hashes
O(n + k×m) — O(n) sliding window + O(km) to hash all patterns
O(n×k)
quiz.explanation: Build a hash set of all k pattern hashes: O(k×m). Slide window through text: O(n) comparisons (hash set lookup O(1) per window). Verification on matches: O(m) per hit but expected O(1) hits. Total: O(n + km).

quiz.question: Longest Duplicate Substring: binary search + Rabin-Karp. Why binary search on length?
options: Arbitrary choice — linear scan also works
Monotonicity: if a duplicate of length L exists, duplicates of length L-1 also exist. Binary search finds the maximum L in O(log n) steps.
Binary search reduces the hash collision probability
Linear scan would be O(n³) which is too slow
quiz.explanation: Monotonic property: existence of duplicate of length L implies duplicate of length L-1 (take any prefix). Binary search on L: O(log n) iterations, each O(n) rolling hash pass. Total: O(n log n). Linear scan: O(n²) rolling hash passes = O(n²) total.

theory_mcq.question: The ROLLING HASH update removes the leftmost character and adds a new rightmost character in O(1). Why is the formula `winHash = (winHash - text[i]*highPow)*BASE + text[i+m]` O(1)?
options: The formula requires scanning all m characters in the window

The polynomial hash of window [i..i+m-1] is `Σ text[j]*BASE^(m-1-j+i)` for j in [i..i+m-1]; shifting to [i+1..i+m]: subtract the CONTRIBUTION OF text[i] (which is text[i]*BASE^(m-1)*1 = text[i]*highPow), multiply remaining by BASE (shifts powers up by 1), then add text[i+m] (the new character at power 0); this recurrence uses PRECOMPUTED highPow = BASE^(m-1) and three arithmetic operations — completely independent of m; the O(1) per step is what makes rolling hash efficient
O(1) is achieved by caching previously computed window hashes
The update is O(1) only when BASE is a power of 2
theory_mcq.explanation: Matching the lesson's code: `winHash = (winHash - text[i]*highPow%MOD + MOD) % MOD; winHash = (winHash*BASE + text[i+m]) % MOD` — two operations per step: remove oldest character's contribution (subtract text[i]*BASE^(m-1)), multiply everything by BASE (shifting existing hash), add new character; three O(1) arithmetic operations regardless of window size m.

theory_mcq.question: Rabin-Karp is O(n+m) AVERAGE but O(nm) WORST CASE. What causes the worst case?
options: The worst case occurs when the text is very long

HASH COLLISIONS cause the worst case: when many windows have the SAME HASH as the pattern (false positives), each requires O(m) character-by-character verification; if every window has the same hash (e.g., all-'a' text and pattern with pathological hash), the verification runs m times for each of n-m+1 windows = O(nm); in practice, a good hash function (polynomial with large prime MOD) makes collisions extremely rare; DOUBLE HASHING (two independent hashes) virtually eliminates false positives
The worst case occurs when the pattern is not found
The worst case occurs when BASE is too small
theory_mcq.explanation: Matching the lesson's concept: 'O(n+m) average, O(nm) worst case' and 'Hash collision: two different strings with the same hash (false positive)' — the verification step `if(text.slice(i,i+m)===pattern)` is O(m) and is triggered on every hash match; if every window has the same hash as the pattern, the total verification cost is O((n-m)*m) = O(nm); good hash functions make this practically O(n+m).

logic_mcq.question: In rolling hash, `highPow = BASE^(m-1)` is precomputed BEFORE the sliding loop. Why is BASE^(m-1) specifically needed (not BASE^m or BASE^(m-2))?
options: BASE^(m-1) is arbitrary; any power would work

The leftmost character text[i] in the window of size m contributes `text[i] * BASE^(m-1)` to the total hash (since it's multiplied by BASE for each of the m-1 other characters to its right); removing it requires SUBTRACTING text[i]*BASE^(m-1); highPow = BASE^(m-1) is exactly this contribution weight; BASE^m would be one power too high (not the leftmost character's weight); BASE^(m-2) would be one too low; the correct removal formula is `winHash -= text[i] * BASE^(m-1)`
BASE^(m-1) prevents integer overflow during hash computation
BASE^(m-1) is needed to maintain the hash modulo MOD correctly
logic_mcq.explanation: In the polynomial hash `Σ text[j]*BASE^(m-1-j+i)`, the leftmost character text[i] has exponent m-1-i+i = m-1; therefore text[i]'s contribution is text[i]*BASE^(m-1) = text[i]*highPow; subtracting this removes exactly the leftmost character; using BASE^m or BASE^(m-2) would incorrectly over- or under-subtract the leftmost character's contribution.

logic_mcq.question: For MULTI-PATTERN search with the same pattern length, Rabin-Karp uses a MAP of pattern hashes instead of iterating each pattern. What is the time complexity advantage?
options: Map lookup is O(1) regardless of the number of patterns

With k patterns (all same length m): naive comparison of each window against all k patterns = O(nm) per window × n windows = O(knm) total; Rabin-Karp with Map: compute 1 rolling hash per window (O(1)) then Map lookup (O(1)) — only verify when there's a hash match; for k patterns, average verification cost remains O(m) per collision (rare); total ≈ O(n + km) for building hashes; pattern hashes built in O(km); scanning with O(n) rolling hash; vs O(nm) per pattern individually (O(knm) total) — the improvement is O(k) fold
The Map reduces time to O(n) regardless of pattern lengths
Multi-pattern search with Map is O(n log k) via binary search
logic_mcq.explanation: Matching the lesson's concept: 'Multiple patterns: store pattern hashes in a Set; O(n) scan with O(1) Set lookup' — the key insight: after one O(n) rolling hash scan, each window's hash is checked against a Set/Map of k pattern hashes in O(1); naively, comparing each window against k patterns would be O(knm); the hash-based approach reduces this to O(n + km) preprocessing + O(n) scanning.

syntax_mcq.question: In rolling hash update, `winHash = (winHash - text[i]*highPow%MOD + MOD) % MOD`. Why is `+ MOD` added before the final `% MOD`?
options: + MOD is added for efficiency; it has no effect on the result

PREVENTS NEGATIVE MODULAR RESULT: in JavaScript, `%` with negative operands can return negative values; `winHash - text[i]*highPow%MOD` might be negative if the subtracted value exceeds winHash; for example, winHash=5 and text[i]*highPow%MOD=10: result=-5; `-5%MOD` in JavaScript =-5 (negative, not the correct positive modular value); adding MOD first ensures the intermediate result is non-negative before applying %MOD: (-5+MOD)%MOD = (MOD-5)%MOD = correct positive modular value
+ MOD is needed to convert the result from float to integer
+ MOD prevents hash collisions by shifting all values by MOD
syntax_mcq.explanation: JavaScript's `%` operator returns the remainder with the sign of the dividend (not always positive); for correct modular arithmetic where results must be in [0, MOD), we must handle negative intermediates; `(x + MOD) % MOD` where x might be negative ensures a non-negative result; this is the standard modular arithmetic pattern in JavaScript for subtraction operations.

lessons.title: Z-Algorithm
lessons.objective: Implement the Z-algorithm to compute the Z-array in O(n) and apply it to string matching as an alternative to KMP, understanding the Z-box maintenance that gives O(n) complexity.
concepts: Z-array: Z[i] = length of longest substring starting at i that matches a prefix of s
Z[0] = length of s (by convention, or undefined)
Z-box [l, r]: current rightmost matching window
O(n): the Z-box right boundary r only moves rightward, giving amortised O(1) per step
Pattern matching: concatenate p + '$' + t; Z[i] = m means pattern starts at i-m-1
Equivalent to KMP for pattern matching: same O(n+m) complexity
Z-box invariant: s[l..r] matches s[0..r-l]
Case splits: i inside Z-box (use previous Z value), i outside Z-box (naive extend)
lessons.explanation: The Z-algorithm computes Z[i] for each position i: the length of the longest substring of s starting at i that matches a prefix of s. Example: for 'aabxaa', Z = [_,1,0,0,2,1] where Z[4]=2 because s[4..5]='aa' matches s[0..1]='aa'. The Z-box [l, r] is the rightmost matching window seen so far (Z[l..r] = prefix of s). For each new position i: if i is within [l, r], we can initialise Z[i] using the previously computed Z[i-l] (the corresponding position in the prefix): Z[i] = min(r-i+1, Z[i-l]), then extend naively. If i is outside [l, r], compute Z[i] naively (extend character by character). After each Z[i] is computed, update [l, r] if i + Z[i] - 1 > r. The Z-box's right boundary r only moves right throughout the algorithm, giving O(n) total. Pattern matching: concatenate pattern + '$' + text. Any Z[i] == m (pattern length) indicates a match.
lessons.analogy: The Z-algorithm is like using a sliding 'match window' to avoid re-comparing already-known matching regions. Once you know that the substring at position l matches the prefix of length r-l+1, when you reach any position inside this window, you can immediately read your earlier answer (from the Z-array of the prefix part) without re-comparing. The window only slides right, so each character is compared at most twice — once to extend a window, once to be within a window.

code_example.explanation: The separator '$' between pattern and text prevents Z[i] from accidentally counting across the boundary. Without it, Z[i] at a position spanning the pattern-text boundary could give Z[i] > m even when the full pattern doesn't match at that text position. The '$' character (or any character not in the alphabet) resets the comparison at the boundary.

common_mistakes: Not using a separator character between pattern and text in Z-search — without a separator, Z values can count across the pattern-text boundary giving false matches; always use a unique character like '$' that does not appear in either string
Using Z[i] >= m instead of Z[i] == m for match detection — Z[i] > m would mean the match extends past the pattern end, which cannot happen since the separator stops it; Z[i] == m is exactly right
Computing Z[0] correctly — Z[0] = length of s by convention (or 0 depending on implementation); the choice affects pattern matching detection but both conventions work if consistently applied
lessons.interview_relevance: The Z-algorithm is tested at companies with competitive programming interview styles. It directly solves 'find all occurrences of pattern in text' and 'find the longest substring that is both prefix and suffix' in O(n). Minimum Period of a String can be found using Z: the string s has period p if Z[p] >= n-p, meaning s[p..n-1] matches the first n-p characters of s.
lessons.mini_challenge: Implement zFunction and verify Z('aabxaab')=[7,1,0,0,3,1,0]. Implement zSearch and verify it returns [0,5,7] for ('aabxaabaab','aab'). Then compare Z-algorithm to KMP: implement both and run them on the same test case. Measure which is simpler to implement. Finally, solve Minimum Period of a String: for string s of length n, find the minimum period p. Use the Z-array: the minimum period is the smallest p where Z[p] >= n-p.

flashcards.front: Z-algorithm: what does it compute?
flashcards.back: Z[i] = length of the longest substring starting at position i that is also a prefix of S. Z[0] is conventionally set to 0 or S.length. Z[1..n-1] give 'how much of S[i..] matches S[0..]'. Computed in O(n) using the Z-box optimisation.

flashcards.front: Z-algorithm: the Z-box [l, r]?
flashcards.back: The Z-box maintains the rightmost interval [l, r] such that S[l..r] is a prefix of S. For each new position i: if i ≤ r (inside Z-box): Z[i] = min(r-i+1, Z[i-l]) as a starting point, then extend. If i > r: compute Z[i] naively and update [l, r] if Z[i] > 0.

flashcards.front: Z-function for pattern matching: how?
flashcards.back: Concatenate P + '$' + T (where '$' is a separator not in alphabet). Compute Z on this string. Any position in the T-part where Z[i] = |P| is a match. The separator ensures Z[i] never exceeds |P| for positions in T.

flashcards.front: Z-algorithm vs KMP: structural comparison?
flashcards.back: KMP uses the failure function (prefix-suffix matching of the PATTERN). Z-function computes prefix matches at EVERY position of the full string. Both are O(n+m) for pattern matching. Z-function is often simpler to understand (no failure function needed) but uses more space (concatenated string).

flashcards.front: Z[i] = 0: what does it mean?
flashcards.back: S[i] ≠ S[0]. No prefix of S matches at position i. For pattern matching (P$T): Z[i]=0 at position in T means T doesn't start with P[0] at this position.

flashcards.front: Z-algorithm time complexity: why O(n)?
flashcards.back: The right boundary r of the Z-box only INCREASES (never decreases). Each character contributes at most once to extending r. Once r has been advanced to position j, Z[j] is known without re-examination. Total work: O(n).

quiz.question: Z-function of 'AABXAA': Z[4]=?
quiz.explanation: Z[4]: compare S[4..] with S[0..]. S[4]='A'=S[0]='A' → extend. S[5]='A'=S[1]='A' → extend. S[6] doesn't exist. Z[4]=2. ('AA' starting at position 4 matches the prefix 'AA'.)

quiz.question: Pattern matching via Z: concatenate 'ABAB$ABABAB'. At which positions in T does Z[i] = 4 (=|P|)?
options: Positions 5 and 7 (T positions 0 and 2)
Position 5 only
Positions 5, 7, 9
Position 9 only
quiz.explanation: P='ABAB' (len=4), separator='$', T='ABABAB'. Concatenated: 'ABAB$ABABAB'. Z[5]: 'ABABAB' vs 'ABAB$': match 'ABAB' (4 chars), then '$' ≠ 'A', Z[5]=4. Z[7]: 'ABAB' vs 'ABAB$': Z[7]=4. Z[9]: 'AB' vs 'AB$': Z[9]=2 ≠ 4. Matches at T positions 0 and 2 (concat indices 5 and 7).

quiz.question: Z-box [l,r]: at position i < r, Z[i] starts as min(r-i+1, Z[i-l]). Why the min?
options: To avoid negative values
Z[i-l] is Z of the same position within the previous Z-box — but if Z[i-l] would extend beyond r, we can only guarantee up to r; need to verify beyond r manually
min ensures Z[i] ≤ |pattern|
To prevent infinite loops
quiz.explanation: If Z[i-l] < r-i+1: Z[i]=Z[i-l] exactly (fully within current Z-box, no need to verify further). If Z[i-l] ≥ r-i+1: we know at least r-i+1 characters match (within Z-box), but we must extend manually beyond r to find the true Z[i]. Hence min(r-i+1, Z[i-l]) as the starting point.

quiz.question: Z-function of 'AAAA': Z[2]=?
quiz.explanation: Z[2]: compare S[2..] with S[0..]. S[2]='A'=S[0], S[3]='A'=S[1], S[4] doesn't exist. Z[2]=2. (The suffix 'AA' starting at position 2 matches the prefix 'AA'.)

complexity_summary.vs_kmp: Both O(n+m); Z-function avoids explicit failure function; KMP is in-place for text

theory_mcq.question: The Z-box [l, r] is maintained so `s[l..r] == s[0..r-l]`. Why does maintaining this Z-box reduce the Z-array computation from O(n²) to O(n)?
options: The Z-box stores previously computed results, eliminating redundant work

The Z-BOX ENCODES PREVIOUSLY VERIFIED MATCHES: when processing position i < r, we know s[i..r] == s[i-l..r-l] (shifts the Z-box context to position i); the Z-value at position i-l (Z[i-l]) tells us how far the match at position i-l extends from the start; we can initialise Z[i] = min(r-i, Z[i-l]) for FREE (no character comparisons); only when we need to extend BEYOND r do we make new comparisons; crucially, r only MOVES RIGHTWARD — each character is 'discovered' at most once in the while loop, giving O(n) total comparison work across all positions
The Z-box limits each computation to O(log n) steps
The Z-box is a lookup table of all possible substring matches
theory_mcq.explanation: Matching the lesson's concept: 'O(n): the Z-box right boundary r only moves rightward, giving amortised O(1) per step' — the amortised argument: r is monotonically non-decreasing; each rightward advance of r corresponds to a new character comparison; total rightward moves of r <= n = total character comparisons across all iterations; hence O(n) total.

theory_mcq.question: For Z-algorithm pattern matching, the concatenated string is `pattern + '$' + text`. Why is the separator '$' necessary?
options: '$' is a convention; any character works as separator

THE SEPARATOR PREVENTS INCORRECT CROSS-BOUNDARY MATCHES: if pattern='aa' and text='aaa', without separator: combined='aaaaa'; Z[2]=3 (matches 3 characters starting at pos 2), but we only want Z[i] exactly equal to m=2 for a pattern match; without separator, Z values might blend the pattern-text boundary; with '$' (a character not in pattern or text): the Z-value at any position in the text portion CANNOT EXCEED m (since '$' blocks the extension at position m in the pattern); Z[i]==m gives an exact pattern match; the separator enforces Z[i] ≤ m for all text positions
The separator '$' encodes the end of pattern for correct pointer jumping
'$' is needed to ensure the Z-array has exactly n+m+1 elements
theory_mcq.explanation: Matching the lesson's concept: 'Pattern matching: concatenate p+"$"+t; Z[i]=m means pattern starts at i-m-1' — the separator's key property: if '$' doesn't appear in pattern or text, Z[i] for positions in the text part can NEVER extend past the '$' separator; therefore Z[i] ≤ m for all positions in the text part; equality Z[i]==m precisely identifies pattern matches.

logic_mcq.question: For `zFunction('aabxaab')`, the result is [7,1,0,0,3,1,0]. Verify Z[4]=3.
options: Z[4]=3 because s[4..6]='aab' matches s[0..2]='aab' ✓ — both are 'aab'
Z[4]=3 because 'aabxaab' has 3 'a' characters after position 4
Z[4]=3 because the Z-box extends from position 4 to position 6
Z[4]=3 because s[4]='a' starts a new Z-box of length 3
logic_mcq.explanation: Confirmed by direct execution: Z[4]=3; s='aabxaab'; s[4..6]='aab' (s[4]='a', s[5]='a', s[6]='b'); s[0..2]='aab'; comparing: s[4]='a'==s[0]='a' ✓, s[5]='a'==s[1]='a' ✓, s[6]='b'==s[2]='b' ✓; extension would check s[7] but string ends; Z[4]=3 ✓.

logic_mcq.question: KMP and Z-algorithm both solve the same pattern matching problem in O(n+m). What is the PRIMARY conceptual difference in their intermediate data structures?
options: KMP uses a stack; Z-algorithm uses a queue

KMP FAILURE FUNCTION (lps): for each position in the pattern, stores 'how many characters we've already matched as both prefix and suffix' — encodes SUFFIX-PREFIX OVERLAP for jumping the pattern pointer on mismatch; Z-ARRAY: for each position in the full string, stores 'how long a prefix of the full string starts here' — encodes EXPLICIT PREFIX MATCH LENGTHS; KMP's lps is pattern-centric (about the pattern's internal structure); Z-array is position-centric (about each position's relationship to the string's prefix)
Z-algorithm uses O(n+m) space while KMP uses O(m) space
KMP handles overlapping matches; Z-algorithm does not
logic_mcq.explanation: Matching the lesson's comparison: 'KMP: failure function encodes suffix-prefix overlaps (used for pattern pointer jumping); Z: Z-array encodes longest prefix match from each position' — both are equivalent for pattern matching but encode information differently; Z-array is often considered more intuitive (direct prefix match length); lps is more compact (pattern-only) but less directly interpretable.

syntax_mcq.question: In `zFunction`, `Z[0] = n` is set by convention. Why is Z[0] not computed by the same algorithm as other Z values?
options: Z[0] is special because the string starts at position 0 and has no Z-box to reference

Z[0] WOULD BE UNDEFINED if computed naively: Z[0] = 'length of prefix of s matching s[0..∞]' = the entire string (s matches itself); the while loop for Z[0] would compare s[0] with s[0], s[1] with s[1], etc. — always matching until end of string = n; setting Z[0]=n directly is correct by definition AND avoids the loop; additionally, many Z-algorithm formulations skip Z[0] entirely (start from i=1) since Z[0]=n is definitionally true and the Z-box [l,r] starts at l=r=0 without Z[0] affecting it
Z[0]=n prevents the initial Z-box from being set incorrectly
Z[0]=n is needed so that the pattern separator condition Z[i]===m works at position 0
syntax_mcq.explanation: Z[0] represents the length of the longest prefix of s that matches s[0..] — by definition, the entire string s matches itself starting at position 0, so Z[0]=|s|=n; computing this via the while loop would simply count all n characters unnecessarily; the convention Z[0]=n is established upfront and the loop starts from i=1.

lessons.title: Suffix Arrays
lessons.objective: Understand suffix arrays as a sorted list of all suffixes, implement O(n log n) construction, and explain how LCP arrays enable efficient pattern matching and string analysis.
concepts: Suffix array: array of starting indices of all suffixes, sorted lexicographically
SA[i]: starting index of the i-th lexicographically smallest suffix
Naive construction: sort all n suffixes O(n^2 log n) (each comparison O(n))
O(n log n) construction: doubling trick using previously sorted rank pairs
LCP array: lcp[i] = length of longest common prefix between SA[i-1] and SA[i]
Pattern matching with SA: binary search on SA in O(m log n)
Applications: longest repeated substring, number of distinct substrings
O(n log n) is sufficient for most interviews; O(n) SA-IS algorithm exists
lessons.explanation: A suffix array of string s is an array SA where SA[i] is the starting index of the i-th lexicographically smallest suffix. Example: for s='banana', SA=[5,3,1,0,4,2] corresponding to suffixes ['a','ana','anana','banana','na','nana']. Naive O(n² log n): sort all n suffixes using string comparisons (each O(n)). O(n log n) construction (doubling): start with rank[i] = character code of s[i]. In each doubling step, sort suffixes by their (rank[i], rank[i+2^k]) pairs using radix sort. After log(n) doublings, ranks are fully determined. The LCP array (Longest Common Prefix): lcp[i] = length of the longest common prefix between the (i-1)-th and i-th sorted suffixes. Used for: finding the longest repeated substring (max LCP value), counting distinct substrings (n*(n+1)/2 - sum(LCP)), and suffix array-based pattern matching in O(m log n) via binary search. Pattern matching: binary search on SA; compare pattern against suffixes at the midpoint.
lessons.analogy: A suffix array is like an alphabetically sorted index of all 'tail sections' of a book. Want to find where the word 'ana' appears? Binary search the suffix index for entries starting with 'ana'. All occurrences are contiguous in the sorted order (since they share the same prefix), so a binary search finds the range in O(m log n). The LCP array tells you how much consecutive index entries overlap — useful for finding the most repeated phrase.

code_example.explanation: Kasai's algorithm builds the LCP array in O(n) using the key observation: if lcp[rank[i]] = h (suffix i and the previous suffix in SA share h characters), then lcp[rank[i+1]] >= h-1 (the suffix starting one position later shares at least h-1 characters). This allows h to be decremented by at most 1 per iteration, giving O(n) total increments and decrements of h.

common_mistakes: Using s.slice(a) < s.slice(b) for suffix comparison in the sort — this creates O(n) strings per comparison, making the total sort O(n² log n); for large n, use rank-based comparison
Computing lcp[0] incorrectly — lcp[0] = 0 by convention (there is no predecessor to SA[0]); Kasai's algorithm correctly starts from rank[i] > 0

Confusing suffix array (indices) with the sorted suffixes themselves — SA contains indices into the original string, not the suffix strings; always slice s[SA[i]:] when you need the actual suffix text
lessons.interview_relevance: Suffix arrays appear in competitive programming and bioinformatics-focused companies (genome sequencing, DNA pattern matching). Longest Duplicate Substring (#1044) can be solved with SA+LCP in O(n log n). The ability to explain SA construction (doubling technique) and LCP (Kasai's algorithm) demonstrates depth of string algorithm knowledge that distinguishes senior candidates.

flashcards.front: Suffix Array: what does it store?
flashcards.back: An array SA where SA[i] = starting index of the i-th LEXICOGRAPHICALLY SMALLEST suffix of string S. Example: S='banana', suffixes sorted: 'a','ana','anana','banana','na','nana'. SA=[5,3,1,0,4,2].

flashcards.front: Suffix Array construction: naive O(n² log n) approach?
flashcards.back: Generate all n suffixes as strings. Sort them using comparison-based sort: O(n log n) sorts × O(n) comparison per sort = O(n² log n). Not practical for n > 10^4. O(n log n) algorithms (SA-IS, DC3) build the suffix array directly.

flashcards.front: LCP Array: what is it and how does it relate to suffix array?
flashcards.back: lcp[i] = length of the Longest Common Prefix between SA[i] and SA[i-1] (adjacent suffixes in sorted order). Computed in O(n) using Kasai's algorithm after building the suffix array. Together SA+LCP enable many string queries in O(n) space and O(log n) or O(1) query time.

flashcards.front: Suffix Array: how to find all occurrences of pattern P in O(m log n)?
flashcards.back: Binary search on the suffix array: find the leftmost and rightmost positions where the suffix starts with P (compare P with SA[mid]-th suffix of S). O(log n) iterations × O(m) comparison = O(m log n). With the LCP array: O(m + log n).

flashcards.front: Longest Common Substring of two strings using suffix array?
flashcards.back: Concatenate S1 + '#' + S2 (separator). Build suffix array + LCP array. The longest common substring = max LCP value where SA[i] and SA[i-1] come from DIFFERENT original strings (one < |S1|, one > |S1|). O((|S1|+|S2|) log n) or O(n) with O(n) SA construction.

flashcards.front: Number of distinct substrings using SA+LCP?
flashcards.back: Total substrings = n×(n+1)/2. Subtract duplicates: each suffix SA[i] has lcp[i] characters in common with the previous suffix (already counted). Distinct substrings = n×(n+1)/2 - Σlcp[i]. O(n) after SA+LCP construction.

quiz.question: LCP array for SA=[5,3,1,0,4,2] of 'banana': lcp[1]=? (between SA[1]=3 and SA[0]=5)
quiz.explanation: SA[0]=5 → suffix 'a'. SA[1]=3 → suffix 'ana'. LCP('a','ana'): compare char by char: 'a'='a', 'n'≠end. LCP=1.

quiz.question: Binary search on suffix array for pattern P='an' in S='banana': which SA range contains all suffixes starting with 'an'?
options: SA[1..2] (indices where suffix starts with 'a' then 'n')

theory_mcq.question: Kasai's algorithm builds the LCP array in O(n) using the KEY INSIGHT that 'LCP can only decrease by 1' between consecutive suffixes in text order. Why can it decrease by at most 1?
options: LCP can decrease by any amount; Kasai's algorithm tracks the exact decrease

KASAI'S LEMMA: if suffix starting at position i has LCP h with its neighbour in SA, then the suffix starting at i+1 has LCP >= h-1 with its neighbour; PROOF: suffix(i) shares h characters with its SA-neighbour suffix(j); removing the first character from both gives suffix(i+1) and suffix(j+1); these still share h-1 characters (the original shared characters minus the first one); in SA order, suffix(i+1) and suffix(j+1) may not be adjacent but their LCP is AT LEAST h-1; therefore the LCP for suffix(i+1) in SA is >= h-1; so h can only decrease by 1 per step → amortised O(n) total decrease → O(n) algorithm
LCP decreases by 1 because we process suffixes in alphabetical order
Kasai's lemma only applies to strings with a small alphabet
theory_mcq.explanation: Matching the lesson's code: `if(h>0) h--` — Kasai's key insight: when moving from suffix i to suffix i+1 (one character shorter), the LCP with the neighbouring suffix in SA can only drop by at most 1; h accumulates upward (via the while loop) and decreases by at most 1 per step; total upward movements ≤ n, total downward ≤ n → O(n) total.

theory_mcq.question: The suffix array for 'banana' is [5,3,1,0,4,2]. What does this represent, and why is suffix array + LCP more powerful than binary search alone?

SA gives only the sorted order; LCP is needed for all string queries
SA+LCP is equivalent to a suffix tree but uses less code
SA[5]=2 means the 6th suffix starts at index 2 in the original string
theory_mcq.explanation: Confirmed by direct execution: SA=[5,3,1,0,4,2] meaning the sorted suffixes are: SA[0]=5→'a', SA[1]=3→'ana', SA[2]=1→'anana', SA[3]=0→'banana', SA[4]=4→'na', SA[5]=2→'nana'; the LCP array lcp=[0,1,3,0,0,2] gives LCP between consecutive sorted suffixes; max(lcp)=3 at index 2 (lcp between 'ana' and 'anana') → longest repeated substring='ana' of length 3; without LCP, finding this would require O(n²) comparisons.

lcp[2]=3 means there are 3 occurrences of 'ana' in 'banana'

logic_mcq.explanation: Confirmed by direct execution: lcp[2]=3; SA[1]=3→'ana' and SA[2]=1→'anana'; common prefix of 'ana' and 'anana' is 'ana' (length 3); lcp[i] stores the length of the longest common prefix between the (i-1)-th and i-th suffixes in sorted order; lcp[2]=3 correctly identifies 'ana' as the shared prefix.

logic_mcq.question: Why does binary search on a suffix array find a pattern in O(m log n) rather than O(n log n)?
options: Binary search on SA is O(n log n) because n suffixes are compared

Binary search on SA has O(log n) iterations; each iteration COMPARES the pattern against one suffix requiring O(m) character comparisons (pattern length); if the pattern matches, the suffix has prefix equal to pattern; total: O(log n iterations * m characters each) = O(m log n); this is often faster than KMP's O(n+m) when n>>m and we only need to find one occurrence; for all occurrences, extend the binary search to find the range [lo, hi] in SA where suffixes start with pattern, then all indices in SA[lo..hi] are occurrences
Each binary search step is O(1) because SA is pre-sorted
O(m log n) assumes the pattern appears exactly once
logic_mcq.explanation: Matching the lesson's concept: 'Pattern matching with SA: binary search on SA in O(m log n)' — the binary search makes log n comparisons; each comparison involves checking if pattern ≤ or ≥ the current suffix, which requires comparing up to m characters (pattern length); total O(m log n); for offline queries (many patterns on fixed text), SA-based matching amortises preprocessing.

syntax_mcq.question: The naive suffix array construction uses `SA.sort((a,b) => s.slice(a) < s.slice(b) ? -1 : 1)`. What is the time complexity of this approach and why is it suboptimal?
options: O(n log n) because JavaScript's sort is O(n log n)

O(n² log n): JavaScript's sort performs O(n log n) comparisons; each comparison calls `s.slice(a)` and `s.slice(b)` which are O(n) each (creating new strings and comparing up to n characters); total = O(n log n) comparisons × O(n) per comparison = O(n² log n); the O(n log n) doubling approach avoids this by using integer rank pairs (O(1) to compare) instead of actual suffix strings; the O(n) SA-IS algorithm exists but is rarely needed in interviews
O(n log n) because string comparison uses hashing
O(n²) because sorting n suffixes each of length n
syntax_mcq.explanation: Matching the lesson's note: 'Note: SA.sort with s.slice comparison is O(n² log n)' — the bottleneck is the string comparison: `s.slice(a) < s.slice(b)` creates new strings of length n and compares up to n characters; with O(n log n) sort comparisons, total = O(n² log n); the doubling approach pre-computes ranks so each comparison is O(1), achieving O(n log²n).

lessons.title: Aho-Corasick Multi-Pattern Search
lessons.objective: Explain Aho-Corasick multi-pattern search as a Trie augmented with failure links (analogous to KMP's failure function), and understand why it achieves O(n + total_pattern_length + matches).
concepts: Aho-Corasick: find all occurrences of k patterns in text in O(n + M + matches)
M = total length of all patterns
Trie: insert all patterns, each pattern leaf marked with pattern ID
Failure links: like KMP failure function but for Trie nodes
Failure link of node v: deepest proper suffix of v's string that is also a prefix in the Trie
BFS construction of failure links: O(M)
Text search: traverse Trie following characters; on mismatch follow failure links
O(n) search after preprocessing: text pointer never moves backward
lessons.explanation: Aho-Corasick builds a Trie from all patterns and augments it with failure links (similar to KMP's failure function). The failure link of Trie node v points to the longest proper suffix of v's path that is also a prefix in the Trie. These failure links are built using BFS from the root: the failure link of v's child c (on character ch) is found by following v's failure link until a node has a child on ch, or reaching the root. Once built, text search is linear: traverse the Trie following text characters. On a mismatch at node v on character c, follow v's failure link and try again (exactly like KMP jumping the pattern pointer). Whenever a node with a pattern endpoint is reached, report that pattern match. Also follow 'output links' (the closest ancestor via failure links that is a pattern endpoint) to report all patterns ending at the current position. Total complexity: O(M) to build Trie and failure links + O(n + matches) to search. Much more efficient than running KMP k times (O(k*(n+m_i))).
lessons.analogy: Aho-Corasick is like a GPS that routes through multiple simultaneous destinations. The Trie is the road network for all patterns. Failure links are detour routes: if the main road (current Trie path) is blocked (mismatch), the failure link automatically reroutes to the best available road that has some progress already made. The BFS preprocessing builds all detour routes upfront so the search drives smoothly at O(n) speed.

code_example.explanation: The output link (child.output = child.output.concat(child.fail.output)) is the key to reporting overlapping pattern matches. When 'she' ends at position i, the failure chain might lead to a node where 'he' also ends. Without concatenating outputs along the failure chain, the 'he' match would be missed. This is the Aho-Corasick 'output link' mechanism.

common_mistakes: Not following failure links when no child exists during search — the search must follow failure links when the current Trie node has no child for the current text character; without this, the search stops at the first mismatch
Not inheriting output along failure links — when a failure link leads to a node with its own pattern endpoint, that match must also be reported; concatenating outputs during BFS build handles this

Building failure links incorrectly for root's direct children — root's children should have fail = root (not null); using null as the failure link for root's children requires special-casing in the search
lessons.interview_relevance: Aho-Corasick appears in competitive programming and NLP/search companies for multi-pattern matching. Word Search II from Level 1 Module 8 (Trie + grid backtracking) is a simpler variant; Aho-Corasick generalises this to linear-time search. The conceptual understanding (Trie + KMP failure links) demonstrates advanced string algorithm knowledge that distinguishes candidates at algorithm-focused companies.

flashcards.front: Aho-Corasick: failure link for a node?
flashcards.back: The failure link of a trie node v (representing string s) points to the node representing the LONGEST PROPER SUFFIX of s that is also a prefix of some pattern. Like KMP failure function but for multiple patterns simultaneously. Computed with BFS in O(Σm_i).

flashcards.front: Aho-Corasick: output links?
flashcards.back: When at trie node v after matching some text, output links point to all patterns that are SUFFIXES of the current text position. Computed by following failure links transitively. Without output links, patterns that are suffixes of other patterns would be missed.

flashcards.front: Aho-Corasick: searching the text?
flashcards.back: Simulate walking the trie on the text. At each character: follow trie edge if exists; else follow failure link repeatedly until trie edge found or at root. When at a node: traverse output links to report all patterns ending here. O(n + output) text traversal.

flashcards.front: Aho-Corasick vs running KMP k times: complexity comparison?
flashcards.back: K × KMP: O(n×k + Σm_i) — scan text for each pattern. Aho-Corasick: O(Σm_i) build + O(n + output) search. For k large patterns: Aho-Corasick is O(n + output) vs O(nk). For k=1: equivalent to KMP.

flashcards.front: Aho-Corasick trie build vs failure link build?
flashcards.back: TRIE BUILD: insert all k patterns character by character → O(Σm_i). FAILURE LINKS: BFS from root, for each node v with parent p and edge character c: follow p's failure link until a node with a c-child is found (or reach root). O(Σm_i) total since BFS visits each trie node once.

theory_mcq.question: In Aho-Corasick, the FAILURE LINK of node v points to 'the deepest proper suffix of v's string that is also a prefix in the Trie'. How is this analogous to KMP's failure function?
options: Failure links and KMP lps are unrelated concepts

KMP lps[j]: for pattern[0..j], lps[j] = length of longest proper prefix = suffix; on mismatch at j, jump pattern pointer to lps[j]; A-C failure link: for Trie node representing string S, fail link points to the node representing the longest proper SUFFIX OF S that is also a PREFIX OF SOME PATTERN in the Trie; on mismatch (character c not in children), follow fail link and try c again; BOTH encode 'how much of previous progress can be reused after a mismatch'; A-C generalises KMP from one pattern to multiple patterns by building the lps structure on a Trie instead of a linear array
Failure links and lps both minimise space usage in the data structure
A-C failure links are the reverse of KMP lps values
theory_mcq.explanation: Matching the lesson's concept: 'Failure links: like KMP failure function but for Trie nodes' — the structural analogy: KMP lps[j] = longest proper prefix-suffix of pattern[0..j]; A-C fail[v] = deepest proper suffix of v's string that is a prefix of some pattern; both are computed via BFS/DP and both enable O(text_length) search by avoiding redundant character comparisons.

theory_mcq.question: Why does the Aho-Corasick OUTPUT LINK (inheriting outputs from failure links) enable finding all OVERLAPPING pattern occurrences?
options: Output inheritance is only needed for non-overlapping patterns

OVERLAPPING PATTERNS via output chaining: consider patterns ['he','she','hers'] and text 'shers'; when we finish 'she' at position 2, the node's fail link points to the node for 'he' (a suffix of 'she' that's also a pattern prefix); if 'he' is also a complete pattern, it should also be reported; by inheriting outputs: node for 'she' also records 'he' as an output (via fail chain); this captures ALL patterns that are suffixes of the current match position; without output inheritance, 'he' inside 'shers' would be missed
Output links prevent duplicate reporting of the same pattern
Output inheritance is needed to handle patterns of different lengths
theory_mcq.explanation: Matching the lesson's code: `child.output = child.output.concat(child.fail.output)` — when a Trie node N is reached in the text, ALL patterns that end at the current position must be reported; these include: (1) patterns ending exactly at N (N.output), and (2) patterns that are suffixes of N's string (via fail chain outputs); inheriting fail link outputs ensures complete detection of all overlapping occurrences.

logic_mcq.question: For patterns ['he','she','his','hers'] in text 'ahishers', Aho-Corasick finds matches. Which patterns are found?
options: 'his' ending at position 4, 'he' and 'she' at position 5, 'hers' at position 7 — multiple overlapping matches found simultaneously
Only 'she' and 'hers' are found; 'he' and 'his' are not detected
All four patterns are found only if they don't overlap
Only the longest matching pattern at each position is reported
logic_mcq.explanation: Confirmed by the lesson's execution: 'ahishers' contains 'his' (pos 1-3, end=4), 'hers' (pos 4-7, end=7), and via output inheritance: 'he' (ending at pos 5, being a suffix of 'she') and 'she' (ending at pos 5 where text[3..5]='she'); Aho-Corasick detects ALL overlapping occurrences including those embedded within longer matches — this is its key advantage over running KMP once per pattern.

logic_mcq.question: Why does building failure links via BFS (not DFS) ensure correctness?
options: BFS and DFS produce the same failure links; BFS is just faster

BFS PROCESSES NODES BY DEPTH — all nodes at depth d before depth d+1; a failure link from node v (at depth d) points to a node at depth < d; when building fail[v], the node it points to has ALREADY BEEN PROCESSED by BFS (it's at a shallower depth); this guarantees fail[v] is already correctly computed when we need it to compute fail[v.children]; DFS might process a node's children before ensuring the fail links of their ancestors are correct, leading to incorrect failure links
BFS is required because Aho-Corasick only works on trees, not graphs
DFS would create circular failure links
logic_mcq.explanation: BFS level-order traversal ensures that when processing node v at depth d, all nodes at depth < d (including the node pointed to by fail[v]) are already fully computed; this is the same reason BFS is used for building binary lifting tables in LCA — ancestors must be processed before descendants for the DP to be correct.

syntax_mcq.question: In the Aho-Corasick search, `while(node !== this.root && !node.children[c]) node = node.fail` follows failure links. What is the TERMINATION GUARANTEE of this while loop?
options: The loop may run indefinitely for certain inputs

TERMINATION via DECREASING DEPTH: each fail link points to a node at STRICTLY SMALLER DEPTH than the current node; the depth decreases by at least 1 per iteration; depth is bounded below by 0 (the root); therefore the loop terminates in at most depth(node) ≤ M iterations (M = maximum pattern length); at the root, the loop condition `node !== this.root` becomes false, guaranteeing exit; in the worst case (many mismatches), O(M) fail-link traversals per text character, but this is amortised O(1) per character over the full text scan
The loop terminates when c is found in children or the text ends
The loop runs exactly M times for text of length M
syntax_mcq.explanation: The termination argument: fail links form a DAG (directed acyclic graph) strictly decreasing in depth toward the root; the loop terminates when either (1) a node with children[c] is found, or (2) node === root (depth 0, loop condition false); in the worst case, the loop traverses from depth M to depth 0 = M steps, but amortised over all text characters, total fail-link traversals = O(n) by the same argument as KMP's O(n) amortisation.

lessons.objective: Select the correct string algorithm for any pattern matching or string analysis problem within 60 seconds, and map all Module 5 NeetCode 150 problems.
concepts: Single pattern, exact match: KMP or Z-algorithm O(n+m)
Multiple patterns, exact match: Aho-Corasick O(n+M+matches)
Substring search with hash: Rabin-Karp O(n+m) average
All substring analysis: suffix array + LCP O(n log n)
Palindrome prefix/suffix analysis: KMP on s+'#'+reverse(s)
Pattern in circular string: pattern in s+s using KMP/Z
Module 5 NeetCode 150 problems mapped
String algorithms vs DP: string DP for optimal substring, string algorithms for exact matching
lessons.explanation: String algorithm selection follows a clear hierarchy. Single exact match (find pattern in text once or all occurrences): KMP or Z-algorithm, both O(n+m). Multiple exact matches (find multiple patterns simultaneously): Aho-Corasick O(n+M+matches). Hash-based approximate: Rabin-Karp when average-case is sufficient or when multiple patterns have the same length. All substring analysis (find longest repeated substring, count distinct substrings): suffix array + LCP array O(n log n). Palindrome analysis: KMP on the string s + '#' + reverse(s) gives the longest palindromic prefix; palindrome partition uses DP from Level 2. Circular string containment: 'Is pattern in the rotations of s?' reduces to pattern in s+s using KMP. The key distinction from string DP (Level 2): string algorithms find exact matches or analyse substring structure. String DP optimises over substring choices. When a problem asks for 'the best substring' use DP; when it asks for 'find this substring' use KMP/Rabin-Karp.
lessons.analogy: String algorithm selection is like choosing the right tool for document processing. Searching one word in a document: use a search function (KMP). Searching thousands of keywords for spam detection: use a multi-pattern automaton (Aho-Corasick). Plagiarism detection across documents: use rolling hashes (Rabin-Karp). Finding all repeated phrases: build a suffix array. The tool matches the scale and type of the search task.

code_example.explanation: Shortest Palindrome reduces to KMP because the longest palindromic prefix of s is the longest prefix of s that is also a suffix of reverse(s). By building the failure function on s+'#'+reverse(s), lps[-1] gives the length of this palindromic prefix. The '#' separator prevents the KMP from counting across the boundary.

common_mistakes: Using brute-force O(n²) string search when KMP O(n+m) is expected — for competitive programming and certain senior interviews, brute force string search is considered unacceptable; always know KMP
Not knowing when to use Rabin-Karp vs KMP — Rabin-Karp excels at multiple same-length patterns or binary search + hash; KMP is better for general single-pattern matching with worst-case guarantees
Trying to solve Shortest Palindrome with DP instead of KMP — the KMP reduction (lps on s+'#'+reverse(s)) is O(n); DP-based palindrome approaches would be O(n²); KMP is strictly better here
lessons.interview_relevance: Module 5 covers 3 NeetCode 150 problems. Find the Index of First Occurrence (#28) is a direct KMP application. Shortest Palindrome (#214) is a clever KMP reduction that appears at Google and Meta. Longest Duplicate Substring (#1044) combines binary search with rolling hash. These three problems demonstrate mastery of the string algorithm toolkit.

flashcards.front: String algorithm selection: 6 signal → algorithm mappings?
flashcards.back: 1) Single pattern search → KMP or Z-function O(n+m). 2) Multiple pattern search → Aho-Corasick O(Σm+n+out). 3) Substring search with binary search → Rabin-Karp rolling hash. 4) All suffix queries (LCS, distinct substrings, count occurrences) → Suffix Array + LCP. 5) Longest repeated substring → SA+LCP max value. 6) Palindrome-related → Manacher's algorithm (O(n) longest palindromic substring).

flashcards.front: Manacher's algorithm: what does it solve?
flashcards.back: Finds the longest palindromic substring in O(n). Computes P[i] = radius of the longest palindrome centered at each position (for both odd and even lengths using a transformed string with '#' separators). Similar Z-box concept: maintains rightmost palindrome boundary.

flashcards.front: String hashing pitfalls: how to avoid collisions?
flashcards.back: 1) Use a large prime modulus (10^9+7 or 10^9+9). 2) Double hashing (two independent hash functions). 3) Verify with direct comparison on hash matches. 4) Avoid using base as a factor of p (use a prime base like 31 or 37). 5) For competitive programming: random base assignment reduces adversarial input attacks.

flashcards.front: Suffix automaton (SAM): what does it compactly represent?
flashcards.back: The MINIMAL automaton that accepts all SUBSTRINGS of S. O(n) states and transitions. Enables: count distinct substrings O(n), find pattern occurrences O(|P|), LCS of two strings O(|S|+|T|). More powerful than suffix array for some queries but harder to implement.

flashcards.front: Module L3-M05: which algorithms are essential for competitive programming?
flashcards.back: Essential: KMP (universal), Z-function (simpler than KMP), Suffix Array + LCP (handles most hard string problems). Important: Aho-Corasick (multi-pattern), Rabin-Karp (hashing approach). Advanced: Suffix Automaton, Manacher's. Industry: KMP and hashing are most commonly tested in senior interviews.

flashcards.front: Longest Common Substring of two strings: all approaches?
flashcards.back: Naive O(n³). DP 2D table O(nm) time O(nm) space. DP optimised: O(nm) time O(n) space. Suffix Array: concatenate S1#S2, build SA+LCP, find max LCP between suffixes from different strings → O((n+m) log(n+m)) or O(n+m). Suffix Automaton: O(n+m). Rolling hash with binary search: O((n+m) log(n+m)).

quiz.question: Problem: 'Find the minimum number of characters to add to make a string palindrome.' Best approach?
options: KMP: reverse string, find LPS overlap
DP O(n²): LPS length tells minimum insertions = n - LPS
Z-function on S + '#' + reverse(S)
Both B and C work; B uses LPS, C uses KMP-like pattern match
quiz.explanation: Minimum insertions = n - LPS(S) where LPS = Longest Palindromic Subsequence length. Both DP (O(n²)) and KMP on S+'#'+reverse(S) solve this. KMP on S+'#'+reverse(S): the KMP failure function on the LAST character gives the length of the longest palindromic prefix — a different but related quantity.

quiz.question: Suffix array vs KMP for 'find all k occurrences of P in T': which is better?
options: KMP always — O(n+m) search
Suffix Array — O(m log n) search with O(n log n) build. Better if same T is queried many times with different P.
Both identical — same asymptotic complexity
Aho-Corasick — handles multiple patterns
quiz.explanation: KMP: O(n+m) per search, O(m) build per pattern — efficient for single search. Suffix Array: O(n log n) build once, then O(m log n) per pattern query — amortised better for many queries on the same text. For static text with many queries: SA wins. For one-time search: KMP.

quiz.question: Aho-Corasick is to KMP as ____ is to Z-function:
options: Suffix automaton
Manacher's algorithm
The structural analogy doesn't hold
Aho-Corasick IS the multi-pattern generalisation of both KMP and Z-function
quiz.explanation: KMP failure function and Z-function are two ways to build single-pattern matching. Aho-Corasick generalises BOTH to multi-pattern matching by building failure links on a trie (which subsumes both KMP's failure function and Z-function's prefix matching). The analogy: Aho-Corasick is the multi-pattern version of KMP/Z.

quiz.question: For a competitive programming problem: 'given 10^5 queries, each asking if a string of length up to 100 is a substring of a fixed text of length 10^6', best approach?
options: KMP for each query: O(10^5 × 10^6) = too slow
Suffix Array: O(10^6 log 10^6) build + O(100 × log 10^6) per query ≈ O(10^5 × 100 × 20) = 2×10^8 — fast
Aho-Corasick: add all queries as patterns, search once O(10^6 + Σm) — fastest
Both B and C are correct; C is faster by a log factor
quiz.explanation: Suffix Array: O(n log n) build, O(m log n) per query → O(10^5 × 100 × 20) ≈ 2×10^8 (borderline). Aho-Corasick: insert all queries into trie O(10^5 × 100), then search text once O(10^6 + output) — much faster. Both correct, Aho-Corasick wins on this specific problem structure.

theory_mcq.question: The lesson lists Rabin-Karp for 'longest duplicate substring'. Why is BINARY SEARCH combined with rolling hash effective for this problem?
options: Binary search is used to find the substring alphabetically

BINARY SEARCH ON LENGTH: the answer length l satisfies a MONOTONE PROPERTY — if a duplicate substring of length l exists, one of length l-1 also exists; binary search on l; for each candidate length l: use rolling hash to check if any window of size l appears twice in O(n) — total across binary search iterations = O(n log n); without binary search, checking all lengths 1..n would be O(n²); the Rabin-Karp hash enables the O(n) 'does length-l duplicate exist?' check; combining: O(n log n) total
Binary search finds the starting position of the duplicate
Rabin-Karp requires binary search because rolling hash can fail
theory_mcq.explanation: Matching the lesson's concept: 'Rabin-Karp Rolling Hash: longest duplicate substring' — LeetCode #1044 uses binary search on the answer length: if a duplicate of length l+1 exists, one of length l exists (monotone); binary search on length with O(n) RK check per length = O(n log n); the combination is a classic pattern for 'longest X with property Y' problems.

theory_mcq.question: For Shortest Palindrome (#214), the KMP trick concatenates `s + '#' + reverse(s)`. What does the LPS value at the LAST position of this combined string encode?
options: lps[last] encodes the length of the shortest palindrome

lps[last] = LENGTH OF LONGEST PALINDROMIC PREFIX of s: in the combined string `s+'#'+rev(s)`, the last position corresponds to the end of rev(s); a match of length k between a prefix of (s+'#'+rev(s)) and a suffix of (s+'#'+rev(s)) ending here means s[0..k-1] matches the last k characters of rev(s); the last k characters of rev(s) = the reverse of s[0..k-1] = s[0..k-1] is a palindrome; lps[last] = length of longest palindromic PREFIX of s; adding the remaining non-palindromic suffix (reversed) to the front gives the shortest palindrome
lps[last] is always equal to s.length
lps[last] encodes the position of the first palindrome in s
theory_mcq.explanation: Matching the lesson's code: `const palindromicPrefixLen = lps[m-1]` — the '#' separator prevents the lps from crossing the s/rev(s) boundary; the longest prefix of (s+'#'+rev(s)) that equals a suffix of the same string corresponds to s[0..k-1] being a palindrome (since rev(s) at the end is s[0..k-1] reversed); confirmed: shortestPalindrome('abcd')='dcbabcd' and shortestPalindrome('aacecaaa')='aaacecaaa'.

logic_mcq.question: Module 5 has 3 NC150 problems: #28, #214, #1044. What is the UNIFYING PATTERN among these three?
options: All three require O(n) string processing with preprocessing to avoid O(n²) naive solutions
All three use suffix arrays exclusively
All three use Aho-Corasick for multi-pattern matching
All three require greedy string algorithms
logic_mcq.explanation: Matching the lesson's module5_problems: #28 (KMP, O(n+m) vs O(nm) naive), #214 (KMP on concatenated string, O(n) vs O(n²) naive), #1044 (binary search + RK hash, O(n log n) vs O(n²) naive); the common thread: naive solutions are O(n²) due to redundant character comparisons; each algorithm achieves O(n) or O(n log n) by preprocessing or reusing prior computation.

logic_mcq.question: The decision guide maps 'pattern in circular string' to 'KMP on s+s'. Why does doubling the string and running KMP find if pattern p is a rotation of s?
options: Doubling s gives all rotations explicitly, and KMP finds any of them

ALL ROTATIONS OF s ARE SUBSTRINGS OF s+s: any rotation r of s of length n can be written as s[k..n-1]+s[0..k-1] for some k; this sequence appears as a contiguous substring of s+s starting at position k; conversely, any substring of s+s of length n IS a rotation of s; running KMP with pattern p on s+s (length 2n) finds p iff p is a rotation of s; time: O(n+n) = O(n)
s+s contains twice as many characters, making KMP more likely to succeed
Doubling works only when s has odd length
logic_mcq.explanation: The key insight: rotation s[k..n-1]+s[0..k-1] appears as s+s[k..k+n-1]; s+s contains all n rotations of s as substrings of length n; KMP on s+s with pattern p finds p iff p is one of these rotations; this is the elegant O(n) solution to 'is p a rotation of s?' — a classical KMP/Z application.

syntax_mcq.question: In `shortestPalindrome`, `rev.slice(0, s.length - palindromicPrefixLen) + s` builds the result. Why is `rev.slice(0, s.length - palindromicPrefixLen)` the prefix to prepend?
options: The slice gives all of rev(s) which is always prepended

IF palindromicPrefixLen = k, then s[0..k-1] is the longest palindromic prefix of s; we need s to become a palindrome; to achieve this, we prepend the REVERSE OF THE NON-PALINDROMIC SUFFIX s[k..n-1]; the reverse of s[k..n-1] appears at the BEGINNING of rev(s) (since rev(s) = s[n-1]..s[k+1]s[k]s[k-1]..s[0]); specifically rev(s)[0..n-1-k] = reverse(s[k..n-1]); this is `rev.slice(0, n-k)` = `rev.slice(0, s.length-palindromicPrefixLen)`; prepending this ensures the full string becomes a palindrome
The slice removes the palindromic prefix from the reversed string
rev.slice(0, n-k) gives the longest palindromic suffix of s
syntax_mcq.explanation: Matching the lesson's code: `return rev.slice(0, s.length - palindromicPrefixLen) + s` — if lps[last]=k (palindromic prefix length k), the characters s[k..n-1] are NOT part of the palindromic prefix; prepending their reversal makes the full string a palindrome; confirmed: shortestPalindrome('abcd')='dcbabcd' (palindromicPrefixLen=1 for 'a', prepend 'dcb').

module_summary.difficulty: Hard — KMP and Z-function are learnable with practice; suffix arrays require careful index arithmetic; Aho-Corasick requires understanding failure link propagation
core_patterns: KMP lps[i]: longest proper prefix of P[0..i] that is also a suffix; O(m) two-pointer build
KMP search: on mismatch at j, set j=lps[j-1] (never backtrack text pointer); O(n)
Rolling hash: hash_new = (hash_old - T[i]×base^(m-1)) × base + T[i+m] mod p; O(1) slide
Z[i]: longest prefix of S matching at position i; Z-box [l,r] enables O(n) via min(r-i+1, Z[i-l])
Pattern matching via Z: P+'$'+T; find all i where Z[i]=|P|; O(n+m)
Suffix array SA: SA[i] = index of i-th lexicographically smallest suffix; enables O(m log n) pattern search
LCP array: lcp[i] = common prefix length between SA[i] and SA[i-1]; distinct substrings = n(n+1)/2 - Σlcp
Aho-Corasick: trie of patterns + failure links (BFS) + output links; O(Σm) build + O(n+out) search
Aho-Corasick failure link: longest proper suffix of node's string that is a trie prefix
Algorithm selection: single pattern → KMP; multiple patterns → Aho-Corasick; suffix queries → SA+LCP
